catalog_quote: Stress in Gayo is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress is characterised by higher pitch and longer duration than unstressed syllables. Gayo has moraic iambic stress, i.e. primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; stress is shifting when suffixes are added. In this section, primary stress is indicated by a raised stress mark ( ˈ) preceding the syllable. Secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, i.e. the syllable preceding the syllable bearing primary stress, and is indicated by a lowered stress mark ( ˌ): anak [ˌaˈnãk] 'offspring' asu [ˌaˈsu:] 'dog' siut [ˌsɪˈʊt] 'burn' rëje [ˌrɤ:ˈdʒɤ:] 'king' iô [ˌɪˈjo:] 'afternoon' petukel [pəˌtʊˈkəl] 'pumpkin' i-pet-inum-en [ɪpətɪˌnʊˈmə̃n] 'give water (to an animal)' Reduplicated forms (§3.5) have double-word stress ... 2.2.1.2 Phrase stress. new_statements.quote: Klemtoon. Als algemeenen regel kan men aannemen, dat de klemtoon ligt in meerlettergrepige woorden op de voorlaatste syllabe, tenzij deze een ě tot klinker heeft, bv. anak, abang, inö, kōrō, pantak, doch běnjèt, běrndoeng, sěloek, tědoeh. Heeft niet alleen de voorlaatste, doch ook de derde van achteren een ě, dan krijgt deze syllabe een zwak bijaccent, bv. sěděkah, sělěnsoeng, waarin het accent valt op kah en nsoeng doch in beide woorden de syllabe sě een zwak bijaccent heeft. In afleidingen behoudt het grondwoord zijn eigen klemtoon, bv. kěbajakan, rěringkölön, ianggòdné, pěmarén, itirōié, ikělandjangié.
new_statements.translation: Stress. As a general rule one may assume that in polysyllabic words the stress lies on the penultimate syllable, unless that syllable has ě [schwa] as its vowel, e.g. anak, abang, inö, kōrō, pantak, but běnjèt, běrndoeng, sěloek, tědoeh. If not only the penultimate but also the third syllable from the end has an ě, then that syllable receives a weak secondary accent, e.g. sěděkah, sělěnsoeng, in which the accent falls on kah and nsoeng but in both words the syllable sě has a weak secondary accent. In derivations the root word keeps its own stress, e.g. kěbajakan, rěringkölön, ianggòdné, pěmarén, itirōié, ikělandjangié.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress in polysyllables, except that a penult whose vowel is ě (schwa) cannot carry it, in which case stress falls on the final syllable (běnjèt, sěloek, sědě-KAH). Derived words keep the stress of their root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: When both the penult and the antepenult contain ě, the antepenult (sě- in sěděkah, sělěnsoeng) gets a weak secondary accent while the main accent is on the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa penult shifts stress to the final; derivations (prefixed/suffixed forms such as kěbajakan, ikělandjangié) retain the root's stress rather than re-computing it on the derived word.
new_statements.identity_note: Hazeu's dictionary covers the Gayo of the Aceh highlands generally, marking dialect forms (e.g. 'GL' = Gayo Lues) in entries; the Klemtoon paragraph is not dialect-specific. Eades & Hajek (2006) is based on a speaker of the Gayo Lut (Takengon) variety; the JIPA illustration is standard Gayo (gayo1244).

new_statements.quote: In Gayo stress is apparently non-contrastive, and speakers are not aware of any lexical pairs that differ in meaning because of stress placement. In isolation stress normally occurs on the final syllable of the word, e.g. asu /asu/ [aˈsuː] 'dog', serap /sərap/ [səˈɾap̚] 'side', rui /rui/ [ruˈwiː] 'thorn'. The correlates of stress are increased vowel duration, loudness and pitch. [...] it is perhaps better to describe them as occurring variably over a two syllable window (except where the pre-final syllable is open and contains /ə/). [...] Accordingly, Eades (2005) describes primary stress as final, with secondary stress on the penult, e.g. anak /anak/ [ˌaˈnak̚] 'offspring', since this indicates relative evenness of stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule for Gayo is empty; this adds a placement (final primary, penult secondary, non-contrastive, two-syllable window with schwa-penult exclusion). Relative to Hazeu 1907 it differs on the default: Hazeu penult (unless schwa), Eades & Hajek final in isolation; both agree that a schwa penult never carries the stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive; in isolation primary stress is on the final syllable, but the stress correlates (duration, loudness, pitch) spread variably over the last two syllables, so the penult often sounds stressed, especially in connected speech and in Indonesian loans. Where the penult is open with schwa, all correlates sit on the final. Eades (2005) formalises this as final primary + penult secondary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the penult (anak [ˌaˈnak̚]); in longer words it can appear two syllables before the primary stress (muluahni [ˌmuluˈahni]).
new_statements.exceptions: Free variation between penult and final for the same speaker (sara, ama, murantô); Indonesian loans favour the penult (sepakat); with suffix -ni stress tends to stay on the root-final syllable (/mu-luah-ni/ [muluˈahni]); antepenultimate stress in paké=a 'they', attributed to phrasing; older speakers judge final stress native and penult stress Indonesian.
new_statements.identity_note: Hazeu's dictionary covers the Gayo of the Aceh highlands generally, marking dialect forms (e.g. 'GL' = Gayo Lues) in entries; the Klemtoon paragraph is not dialect-specific. Eades & Hajek (2006) is based on a speaker of the Gayo Lut (Takengon) variety; the JIPA illustration is standard Gayo (gayo1244).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress by default in polysyllabic words; a syllable whose vowel is ě (pepet/schwa) is never stressed, so when the penult has ě the stress falls on the final syllable. Derived words keep the stress of their base (stress does not move onto suffixes in his account). A schwa-quality-sensitive penult rule, coded weight-sensitive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: When both penult and antepenult contain ě, the antepenultimate ě-syllable carries a 'zwak bijaccent' (weak secondary accent) while the main accent is final: sěděkah (accent on kah, weak accent on sě), sělěnsoeng (accent on nsoeng, weak accent on sě). Nothing further.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) a penult with ě sends the stress to the final syllable (běnjèt, běrndoeng, sěloek, tědoeh); (ii) derived words keep the base word's own stress (kěbajakan, rěringkölön, ianggòdné, pěmarén, itirōié, ikělandjangié), i.e. no shift onto affixes in his description; (iii) prothetic/on-glide ě syllables (ěmpoes beside mpoes; měněsah from sah) are unstressed by the general statement that an ě syllable is never accented. The rule is hedged 'als algemeenen regel' (as a general rule).
new_statements.identity_note: Hazeu 1907 describes Gajōsch (Gayo) as a whole; the Toelichting (p. VII) distinguishes two main dialects, Laut (L, incl. Döröt) and Gajō-Loeös (GL, incl. to some extent Sěrbödjadi), marked L / GL in the dictionary, and mentions Basa Böbasan and Tampoer; the 'Klemtoon' paragraph is not restricted to a dialect. His informants (Voorbericht p. V) were Njaq Poetéh and Ama-n-Ratoes. Eades 2005 / Eades & Hajek 2006 (the catalog side) describe Gayo Lut (Takengon area).

readall_conflicts: Hazeu (1907) states penultimate stress as the general rule, with the final syllable stressed only when the penult vowel is ě (schwa), a weak secondary accent on a schwa antepenult, and root stress kept in derivations. Eades & Hajek (2006, JIPA) describe stress as non-contrastive, normally final in isolation, with the correlates spread over a two-syllable window so that the penult often sounds stressed in connected speech; they cite Eades (2005) for final primary plus penult secondary, and note that older speakers regard final stress as native and penult stress as Indonesian. The two sources therefore disagree on the default position (penult vs. final) but agree that a schwa penult never carries the stress; Eades & Hajek themselves flag the placement as partly indeterminate and call for further acoustic work (Hajek, Stevens & Eades forthcoming). Hazeu 1907 (p. XII), now read from the open Bodleian scan, states default PENULTIMATE stress with final stress only when the penult vowel is schwa (schwa syllables never stressed; weak secondary accent on a schwa antepenult when penult and antepenult both have schwa; derived words keep the base's stress). This contradicts the final-stress (iambic) placement of Eades 2005 (the catalog record's source, section 2.2.1.1) and of Eades & Hajek 2006 (JIPA, 'stress normally occurs on the final syllable', non-contrastive), which are the modern instrumental/descriptive accounts; e.g. Hazeu marks Anak, Abang, PANtak with penult stress where Eade…

sources.note: Same author plus a phonetician, one year after the grammar: restates final stress in isolation but describes the correlates as spread over a final two-syllable window, often heard as penultimate in connected speech, obligatorily final after an open schwa penult, and not always shifting onto -ni; this both qualifies our 'fixed final, no weight condition' reading of Eades 2005 and largely explains the Hazeu 1907 'penult unless schwa' conflict the record carries.
